common_name: Scarlet Belle Pitcher Plant (Dwarf Red Sarracenia Hybrid)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes and pot into a 1:1 peat moss and perlite mix or pure long-fiber sphagnum; never use fertilized potting soil, and stand the pot in a shallow tray of rain water or distilled water year-round.

directions: Grow in a permanently wet, nutrient-poor acidic medium such as pure sphagnum or a peat-perlite blend, watering only with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water and never fertilizing. Scarlet Belle is a compact, long-registered Sarracenia hybrid prized for pitchers that flush a saturated, near-uniform crimson to scarlet across the entire tube, showing much less green than many taller hybrids and making it a standout in a small bog planter. Its shorter stature keeps it in scale with dish gardens and container bogs, while the pitchers still function like any Sarracenia, luring and digesting insects to supplement the poor bog soil. Give it full, direct sun to develop the deepest red color and let it experience a natural cool winter dormancy with reduced watering, since skipping dormancy will weaken the plant over time.

common_name: Akai Ryu Venus Flytrap (Copper-Red Japanese Cultivar)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes or plant tissue-culture starts in a moist, nutrient-poor, acidic medium of 50/50 peat moss and perlite in full sun; water only with rain water or distilled water, never tap water or fertilizer.

directions: Grow in a mix of 50% peat moss and 50% perlite or sand with no added fertilizer, keep the medium constantly moist with rain water or distilled water, and provide the strongest sun the plant can get. Akai Ryu, whose Japanese name means red dragon, was one of the earlier named all-red flytrap clones in cultivation and tends toward a coppery orange-red rather than the deep burgundy of newer red cultivars such as Red Dragon, with coloring that is more sensitive to light intensity and can fade toward green if grown in lower light. It traps and digests insects the same way as wild-type Venus flytraps, so feeding is optional but not required for survival in a well-lit bog setup. Give it a cold winter dormancy of three to four months around 50 degrees Fahrenheit each year, since skipping this rest period shortens the plant's lifespan.
